newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl ready for summer holiday after difficult year.
newsitem.headline: Kohl ready for summer holiday after difficult year.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, whose popularity is falling as unemployment rises and his squabbling government struggles to find remedies, will have much to reflect on during his four-week summer holiday.

With opinion polls showing Kohl's centre-right coalition would be crushed by an alliance of leftist parties, Kohl heads off to his annual vacation in the Austrian Alps at the end of July carrying more woes than usual in his luggage.

The 67-year-old chancellor will answer some of his critics at a traditional pre-holiday news conference in Bonn on Friday, one of the rare chances the Bonn press corps is given each year to pose questions to Kohl on a wide array of domestic issues.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who lead Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) in voter surveys, have warmed up to the September 1998 election campaign by sarcastically wishing Kohl a pleasant summer holiday on a giant billboard in Bonn.
Complete with a pair of oversize swimming trunks for the burly chancellor, the billboard says it hopes Kohl will soon have a happy holiday that lasts 365 days a year.

Even the normally pro-Kohl business community has signalled its frustration over the sense of stagnation and gridlock in Bonn, where badly needed reforms are often talked to death by powerful lobbies or voted down by the SPD that controls the upper house of parliament.

A survey of 600 German companies to be published in Capital magazine on Friday found 83 percent believe Kohl's government is incapable of making necessary reforms and 73 percent said they were dissatisfied with Kohl's economic policies.

"In the eyes of the captains of industry, the coalition has already lost the election," said the normally staunchly pro-CDU newspaper Die Welt. "The dissatisfaction over the government's work that the managers are showing is an alarm signal."

Even though German exports are booming and the stock market is clocking up new records almost daily, there is a spreading mood of despair in the business community over the government's failure to enact overdue structural reforms.

"The wishes of the companies are not being fulfilled at the moment," Die Welt added. "They want reliability, reforms, more freedom and less bureaucracy. All the attempts to these ends get caught in Bonn's gridlock. Promises to cut costs to employers end up with the exact opposite happening."
The Berlin daily Der Tagesspiegel said the bad marks business managers gave Kohl's government before his summer holiday were "fully deserved."
The 15th year in office for the towering chancellor has been an especially difficult one:
- Unemployment hit a post-war high of more than 11 percent.
- Widening budget deficits have hurt Germany's of meeting fiscal requirements for Europe's planned single currency in 1999.
- A bitter fight in Kohl's conservative party broke open over the criteria for the single currency.
- And Kohl fell on his face with a failed bid to raise cash by revaluing Bundesbank gold reserves.

With the long string of domestic setbacks this year there is little surprise that Kohl's government is on a steep slide in opinion polls. Kohl has made a career of bouncing back from popularity slumps and has won four straight elections.
He doesn't appear very worried at the moment either.
"The coalition is making decisions and taking the needed action," Kohl said confidently in a preface to Union, the CDU's party publication released on Thursday.
"The last weeks were a difficult time for the coalition. But the important message is that the coalition survived this test and proved it can make decisions."

But a poll by the respected Allensbach institute this week found that Kohl's government would be blown away by a coalition of the SPD and the environmental Greens party if general electionns were held now.

The CDU and Bavarian sister party CSU would receive the backing of just 33.2 percent of the voters, down from 33.8 percent a month ago and from 36.5 percent in February -- the last time Kohl's party led the SPD. The Free Democrats, junior coalition partners, would receive 6.4 percent.

The SPD, meanwhile, gained a full percentage point to 37.6 in the last month, according to the monthly Allensbach survey. That was up from 35.5 percent in February and the highest level of backing for Germany's main opposition party since 1993.
The Greens, who would like to form a coalition with the SPD, were slightly lower in the latest Allensbach survey at 13.5 percent compared to 14 percent last month.

And if all that were not bad enough news for Kohl to digest in the Alps, it looks increasingly like the SPD will pick a charismatic figure for a change to challenge Kohl in the 1998 elections -- Gerhard Schroeder, the premier of Lower Saxony.
Schroeder beat Kohl by a 2-to-1 margin in one recent survey.
